questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $10$ and $5.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=10$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=5.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=10:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-10I & =[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-10[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-10I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & 12\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the second principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $13$ and $3.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are ${\lambda }_{1}=13$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3.$
So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=3:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-3I & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 3 \\ 3 & 12\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 3 & 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the first principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $1,$ $2,$ and $9.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=9,\,{\lambda }_{2}=2,\,{\lambda }_{3}=1.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=9:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-9I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -4 & 0 \\ -4 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-9I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
The covariance matrix $C$ of some particular observations is shown below. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Find the third principal component of the data, given that the eigenvalues of $C$ are $8,$ $5,$ and $2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $C$ are called the principal components of the data. If 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}>{\lambda }_{2}>⋯>{\lambda }_{n}
$$

are the eigenvalues of $C$ written in descending order, then: 

- the $1$st principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{1}$ corresponding to the $1$st eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1},$

- the $2$nd principal component is the unit eigenvector ${u}_{2}$ corresponding to the $2$nd eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2},$

- $⋯$

and so on.

In our case, the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix $C,$ in descending order, are 

$$
{\lambda }_{1}=8,\,{\lambda }_{2}=5,\,{\lambda }_{3}=2.
$$

So, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{3}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}C-2I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(C-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=3,$ we get 

$$
{u}_{3}=\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$
